entities.evidence: Yahweh is the personal name of the God who made the animals of the field, the same Yahweh God who brought the woman to the man in Genesis 2:22.
אֱלֹהִים stands in apposition to Yahweh. Together they identify the maker of the animals as the subject of the singular verb עָשָׂה.
The serpent uses אֱלֹהִים for the speaker whose command about eating from the garden’s trees it questions. Genesis 2:16–17 identifies that speaker as Yahweh God.

name_review_base.evidence: Yahweh is the personal name of the God who made the animals of the field, the same Yahweh God who brought the woman to the man in Genesis 2:22.

review.translation: [Now the serpent|0] [was|1] [craftier|2] [than any|3] {other} [beast of|4] [the field|5] [that|6] [Yahweh|8] [God|9] [had made|7]. [And he said|10] [to|11] [the woman|12], “​[Did|15] [God|16] [really|13,14] [say|15], ‘[You must|18] [not|17] [eat|18] [from any|19] [tree of|20] [the garden|21]’?”

analysis.evidence: The verse describes וְהַנָּחָשׁ as more cunning than any beast of the field and then recounts its words to the woman about the trees of the garden. This identifies the serpent in the Eden narrative.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וְ + definite article הַ + common noun, masculine singular absolute.

analysis.evidence: הָיָה agrees with the masculine singular subject הַנָּחָשׁ and links it to the adjective עָרוּם. The comparison introduced by מִכֹּל describes the serpent as more crafty than any other beast of the field.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person masculine singular, with no prefix or suffix
analysis.sense: to be in a state or condition

draft.change: Add עָרוּם “crafty” under ערמ. The candidate under עור covers עָרוֹם “naked.”
draft.definition: Shrewd in choosing words or actions to achieve an aim.
draft.evidence: In Gen. 3:1 the serpent frames God's command as a question about every tree in the garden, drawing the woman into a discussion of the prohibition.

analysis.evidence: הָיָה עָרוּם מִכֹּל describes the serpent as craftier than any other beast of the field. Its opening question shows that craft: it asks whether God forbade eating from any tree, although the command singled out one tree (Gen. 2:16–17).
analysis.morphology: Predicative adjective, masculine singular absolute, agreeing with הַנָּחָשׁ. No prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In עָרוּם מִכֹּל חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה, the serpent is craftier than any other beast of the field. The prefix marks the comparison, and כֹּל extends it to each beast.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular noun in the construct state with prefixed comparative מִן. The נ assimilates to the following כּ.

analysis.evidence: חַיַּת is in construct with הַשָּׂדֶה, forming “beast of the field.” The phrase עָרוּם מִכֹּל חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה describes the serpent as craftier than any wild animal of the field.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular common noun in the construct state.
analysis.sense: wild beast, beast of the field

analysis.evidence: In חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה, “animal of the open country,” הַשָּׂדֶה completes the construct phrase and identifies the habitat of the wild animals with which the serpent is compared.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, masculine singular absolute, with prefixed definite article הַ־.
analysis.sense: open country, the land outside town and house

analysis.evidence: אֲשֶׁר introduces the clause עָשָׂה יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים, “YHWH God made.” Its antecedent חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה, “beast of the field,” supplies the object of עָשָׂה.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected relative particle without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים, the subject is יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים, and the object is understood from חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה, the animals of the field. The clause describes God’s earlier act of making those animals.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third-person masculine singular

analysis.evidence: In אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים, “which Yahweh God made,” יַהְוֶה names the maker of the animals of the field. The following title אֱלֹהִים refers to the same subject.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun without a prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Personal name of the God of Israel

analysis.evidence: In אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים, אֱלֹהִים stands in apposition to יַהְוֶה. The singular verb עָשָׂה identifies YHWH God as the one who made the animals of the field.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural absolute common noun with singular reference.

analysis.evidence: The subject is הַנָּחָשׁ, the serpent. אֶל הָאִשָּׁה identifies the woman as the addressee, and אַף כִּי opens the serpent’s quoted question.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־

draft.change: Add Gen.9.8 as evidence for the existing addressee sense of אֶל at word index 0.
draft.definition: With a verb of speaking, אֶל introduces the addressee.
draft.evidence: In Gen.9.8, וְאֶל בָּנָיו adds Noah’s sons to the hearers already introduced by אֶל נֹחַ.

analysis.evidence: In וַיֹּאמֶר אֶל הָאִשָּׁה, “he said to the woman,” אֶל introduces the woman as the person the serpent addresses.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew preposition without a prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Marks the person or people addressed.

analysis.evidence: וַיֹּאמֶר אֶל הָאִשָּׁה means “he said to the woman.” The phrase identifies the woman as the person the serpent addresses.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular absolute noun with prefixed definite article הָ־.

analysis.evidence: אַף precedes כִּי אָמַר אֱלֹהִים in the serpent’s opening question to the woman. It gives the question the force of “Did God really say …?”
analysis.morphology: Uninflected emphatic particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In אַף כִּי אָמַר אֱלֹהִים, כִּי introduces the proposition the serpent questions, “Is it really the case that God said …?” The words beginning לֹא תֹאכְלוּ give the command attributed to God.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected conjunction with no prefix or suffix. The preceding אַף is a separate word.
analysis.sense: that (what is seen, known or said)

analysis.evidence: In the serpent’s question, אֱלֹהִים is the subject of אָמַר. The words לֹא תֹאכְלוּ (‘you shall not eat’) introduce the prohibition the serpent attributes to God.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third-person masculine singular, with no prefix or suffix

analysis.evidence: In the serpent’s question, אֱלֹהִים is the subject of אָמַר (“said”), a third-person masculine singular verb. It refers to יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים, named earlier in the verse.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural common noun in the absolute state, with singular verbal agreement.

analysis.evidence: In לֹא תֹאכְלוּ, “you must not eat,” לֹא negates the second-person masculine plural imperfect תֹאכְלוּ. The serpent asks whether God issued this prohibition.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected negative particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In the serpent’s question, לֹא negates תֹאכְלוּ, giving “you may not eat.” The phrase מִכֹּל עֵץ הַגָּן identifies the trees of the garden as the source of what is eaten.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, second person masculine plural

analysis.evidence: כֹּל qualifies the singular עֵץ ‘tree’. In the serpent’s question, לֹא תֹאכְלוּ מִכֹּל עֵץ הַגָּן means ‘You shall not eat from any tree of the garden?’
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular construct noun with prefixed מִן ‘from’. The נ assimilates to the following כּ.

analysis.evidence: In עֵץ הַגָּן, “tree of the garden,” הַגָּן completes the construct phrase. The serpent asks about eating from the garden’s trees, which identifies עֵץ as a living tree.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular noun in the construct state, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In מִכֹּל עֵץ הַגָּן, “from any tree of the garden,” עֵץ is in construct with הַגָּן. The garden is where the trees grow.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הַ־ + common noun, singular absolute, common gender, with no suffix.
